'''Michael H Abraham''' (11 December 1931, London – 19 January 2021)<ref name=uclchem>{{cite news|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/chemistry/sites/chemistry/files/2021_newsletter_0.pdf|title=Prof. Michael Abraham|publisher=University College London|newspaper=UCL Chemistry Newsletter|date=2021|page=36|access-date=2024-02-23}}</ref> was an English chemist.<ref name=rjabraham/> He mainly worked in the area of [[physical organic chemistry]], with his research interests being [[hydrogen bonding]], [[solvation]], [[linear free energy relationship]]s (LFER), [[quantitative structure-activity relationship]]s (QSAR) and [[solvent effects|solute-solvent interaction]]s.<ref name=uclchem/><ref name=rsc/><ref name=facprofile>{{cite web|url=http://www.ucl.ac.uk/chemistry/staff/emeritus/michael_abraham|title=Michael Abraham|publisher=University College London|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131216073957/http://www.ucl.ac.uk/chemistry/staff/emeritus/michael_abraham|archive-date=2013-12-16}}</ref><ref name=rjabraham/> A faculty member of [[University College London]] since 1988, Abraham was known within his field for creating the Abraham General Solvation Model.<ref name=facprofile/><ref name=rjabraham>{{cite journal|title=Professor Michael H. Abraham|date=2022-08-09|last=Abraham|first=RJ|journal=[[Journal of Solution Chemistry]]|volume=51|issue=9 |page=974|doi=10.1007/s10953-022-01198-4|url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10953-022-01198-4}}</ref>

==Biography==
Abraham was born 11 December 1931 in London to Judah and Elizabeth Abraham. He was one of four boys. He attended [[Magnus Church of England Academy|Magnus Grammar School]] in [[Newark-on-Trent]] before graduating with [[first class honours]] from [[University of North London|Northern Polytechnic London]], where he studied chemistry, in 1951. He then earned his PhD from University College London (UCL) under [[Alwyn Davies]], and later his [[Doctor of Science|DSc]] in 1974.<ref name=rjabraham/> He became a [[Reader (academic rank)|reader]] at [[Battersea Polytechnic]] until 1988, when he returned to UCL.<ref name=uclchem/><ref name=rjabraham/>

Between 1957 and 1969, Abraham largely focused on the chemistry of [[organometallic]] compounds. Key works done by Abraham and his UCL colleagues include the measuring and calculation of molecular properties of thousands of molecules.{{citation needed|date=March 2024}} These properties include H-bond acidity and basicity, dipolarity and polarisability.<ref>{{cite book|last=Valko|first=Klara|title=Physicochemical and Biomimetic Properties in Drug Discovery|year=2013|publisher=John Wiley|isbn=978-1118770320}}</ref> He received two Ebert awards from the [[American Pharmaceutical Association]]: one in 1992 for his paper ''Role of hydrogen bonding in general anaesthesia'', and again in 2002 for his paper on the "valuation of human intestinal absorption data and subsequent derivation".<ref name=rjabraham/> His work led him to appear on [[Thomson Reuters]]' list of Highly Cited Researchers.<ref name=rsc/>

==Personal life==
Michael Abraham and his wife Elisabeth Mayer (died 1999) had two sons, Benjamin and Jonathan. Elisabeth had also been a PhD student at UCL.<ref name=rjabraham/> Abraham was a hobby landscape painter and held several exhibitions throughout London. Additionally, he enjoyed [[classical music|classical]], particularly [[chamber music|chamber]], music.<ref name=rjabraham/><ref name=uclchem/><ref name=rsc>{{cite web|url=https://blogs.rsc.org/nj/2011/08/23/meet-our-authors-august-2011/?doing_wp_cron=1708748824.5895459651947021484375|title=Meet Our Authors - August 2011|last=Vial|first=Laurent|date=2011-08-23|publisher=NJC Blog, Royal Society of Chemistry|access-date=2024-02-23}}</ref>

Abraham died on 19 January 2021, aged 89.<ref name=rjabraham/>
